title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
description: Brute force to optimized: extracting and rebuilding versus a recursive in-place reversal applied to each fixed-size group, guarded by a look-ahead check.

blocks.text: Given the head of a linked list, reverse the nodes of the list k at a time, and return the modified list. k is a positive integer, and if the number of nodes is not a multiple of k, the LEFT-OUT nodes at the end should remain in their original order (not reversed).

blocks.caption: Every full group of exactly k nodes gets reversed; any leftover partial group at the end is left untouched

blocks.text: The list is processed in consecutive chunks of exactly k nodes; each full chunk gets internally reversed, and chunks are then re-linked together in order. If the very last chunk has fewer than k nodes, it is left exactly as-is.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reversing Fixed-Size Blocks of a Train
blocks.text: Like a train made of many cars, grouped conceptually into blocks of exactly k cars each. Each FULL block of k cars gets internally reversed (the order of cars within that block flips), while the blocks themselves stay in their original sequence relative to each other. If the very last remaining group of cars is smaller than k (not a full block), it is left alone entirely, uncoupled and unreversed.

blocks.caption: Before reversing any group, a look-ahead check confirms whether at least k nodes remain; if not, that trailing group is left untouched

blocks.text: Before reversing everything blindly (or extracting into an array), notice that this problem is exactly the bounded sub-range reversal (as in Reverse Linked List II) applied REPEATEDLY, once per group of k nodes, with a crucial look-ahead check before each reversal.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Reversing a single group of exactly k nodes uses the same standard iterative reversal technique (prev/curr/next pointers) as the classic Reverse Linked List problem, just bounded to k steps instead of the whole list.

Observation 2: BEFORE reversing any group, it must first be confirmed that at least k nodes actually remain from the current position; otherwise that trailing group must be left completely untouched.

Observation 3: After reversing a full group, the ORIGINAL head of that group (now its tail, after reversal) needs its next pointer connected to whatever comes after: specifically, the result of applying this SAME process to the rest of the list.

Observation 4: This naturally suggests a recursive structure: reverse one group, then recursively solve "the rest of the list" and attach the result, or equivalently, an iterative version using an explicit stack of "previous group's tail" pointers.

Recognizing this as "apply Reverse Linked List II's technique repeatedly, guarded by a look-ahead check" directly connects this problem to two already-covered techniques in this category.
This is the standard iterative reversal technique bounded to groups of exactly k nodes, repeated across the list, with a look-ahead check guarding the final possibly-partial group.
Extract every value into an array, reverse each full k-sized chunk of the array in place, leaving any trailing partial chunk untouched, then rebuild the list from the modified array.

items: Walk through the list, collecting every value into an array.
Repeatedly reverse each consecutive chunk of exactly k elements, advancing by k each time, stopping once fewer than k elements remain.

codes.python:
def reverse_k_group(values, k):
    result = values[:]
    i = 0
    while i + k <= len(result):                                            # only reverse FULL groups of exactly k
        result[i:i + k] = reversed(result[i:i + k])
        i += k
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(reverse_k_group([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The loop condition (i + k <= size) naturally stops BEFORE processing any trailing group smaller than k, correctly leaving it untouched.
Reversing each chunk directly in the array mirrors exactly what the linked-list version must achieve using pointer re-linking instead.

blocks.text: Correctly reverses every full group of k while leaving any trailing partial group untouched, since the loop bound naturally excludes it.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to collect plus one to reverse chunks and rebuild.
Space: O(n), for the intermediate array and the entirely new set of nodes created.

Limitation: extracting values and creating brand new nodes ignores that the EXISTING nodes can simply be re-linked in place, achieving the same result with O(1) extra space (aside from recursion, if used).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rebuilds an entirely new list. Instead, first check (via a look-ahead walk) whether at least k nodes remain; if not, return the list unchanged from here. Otherwise, reverse exactly k nodes using the standard iterative technique, then RECURSIVELY apply this same process to whatever comes after, and connect the (now-tail) original head of this group to that recursive result.

Define hasKNodes(node, k): walk up to k steps, confirming k nodes exist. In reverseKGroup(head, k): if hasKNodes(head, k) is false, return head unchanged. Otherwise, reverse exactly k nodes (standard prev/curr/next iteration), then set head.next (head is now this group's tail) to reverseKGroup(curr, k) (curr is now positioned right after this group), and return prev (this group's new head).
Reverse each full group of exactly k nodes using the standard iterative technique, recursively handling the rest of the list, guarded by a look-ahead check.

blocks.text: The fully reversed-in-groups result is [2,1,4,3,5], matching the expected output.

codes.python:
def has_k_nodes(node, k):
    count = 0
    while node and count < k:
        node = node.next
        count += 1
    return count == k                                                       # confirms at least k nodes remain from here

def reverse_k_group(head, k):
    if not has_k_nodes(head, k):
        return head                                                         # fewer than k nodes left: leave this final group untouched

    prev, curr = None, head
    for _ in range(k):
        next_node = curr.next
        curr.next = prev                                                    # standard iterative reversal, but bounded to exactly k steps
        prev = curr
        curr = next_node

    head.next = reverse_k_group(curr, k)                                    # head is now this group's TAIL; link it to the next reversed group
    return prev                                                             # prev is now this group's new head


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
    result = reverse_k_group(head, 2)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each node is visited a constant number of times overall (once for the look-ahead check, once for reversal).
Space: O(n/k) for the recursion stack (or O(1) with an iterative version using explicit tracking of each group's boundary).

The look-ahead check (hasKNodes) guarantees that reversal is ONLY ever attempted on a full group of exactly k nodes, correctly leaving any trailing partial group untouched by simply returning it as-is. After each group's standard iterative reversal, the group's ORIGINAL head (now correctly positioned as its tail after reversal) is linked to the result of recursively processing everything after this group, correctly chaining groups together in their original relative order.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Fewer than k nodes remain","hasKNodes returns false; that group is returned completely unchanged"],["Exactly k or more nodes remain","The next k nodes are reversed using the standard technique, then linked to the recursively processed rest"],["The very last group happens to be exactly k nodes","It gets reversed just like any other full group; only a group SMALLER than k is left untouched"]]}

items: hasKNodes performs a bounded walk (stopping early at k), making the look-ahead check itself O(k), not O(n).
The reversal loop is identical in structure to the classic iterative Reverse Linked List, just bounded to exactly k iterations.

head.next = reverseKGroup(curr, k) is the critical connecting step: head is now this group's tail (after reversal), and curr correctly points to the node right after this group, ready to be recursively processed.

blocks.text: Reversing a linked list in fixed-size groups directly reuses the standard bounded-reversal technique (as in Reverse Linked List II), applied repeatedly, guarded by a look-ahead check that correctly leaves any trailing partial group untouched.

items: Forgetting the look-ahead check entirely, which would incorrectly reverse a trailing partial group that should be left untouched.
Connecting a reversed group's tail to the WRONG node (forgetting that the group's original head becomes its tail after reversal, and is what needs the forward connection).
Off-by-one errors in the look-ahead walk, either overcounting or undercounting the k nodes needed.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Reverse in FIXED-SIZE groups, leaving a trailing partial group untouched" points toward the bounded iterative reversal technique applied repeatedly, guarded by a look-ahead check.

items: How would you convert the recursive solution to an iterative one (true O(1) extra space)? Track the previous group's tail explicitly, reconnecting it to each new group's head as groups are processed left to right.

What if the trailing partial group should ALSO be reversed (a common follow-up variant)? Simply remove the look-ahead check's early-return behavior and reverse whatever nodes remain, however many there are.

How does this problem build on Reverse Linked List II? It applies that exact same bounded-reversal mechanic, but repeated across the ENTIRE list in fixed-size groups, rather than just once on a single specified sub-range.
A repeated application of the bounded sub-range reversal technique from Reverse Linked List II, both relying on the same core iterative prev/curr/next reversal mechanic, elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (recursive bounded reversal with look-ahead): O(n) time, O(n/k) space (O(1) with an iterative version).

items: Pattern: Bounded iterative reversal, repeated in fixed-size groups, guarded by a look-ahead check
Core Idea: Confirm at least k nodes remain before reversing each group; after reversing, connect the group's (now-tail) original head to the recursively processed rest of the list
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n/k) recursion stack (O(1) iteratively)
Most Important Observation: A trailing group with fewer than k nodes must be detected via a look-ahead check and left completely untouched
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: If fewer than k nodes remain, stop; else reverse k, then head.next = recurse(rest)
